headline: Deep in the Gut: bass buried in the rip, eels doing the damage
subhead: Cooler water and a hard three-way rig are putting quality bass, a 28-inch sea bass, and keeper fluke on the same stretch of bottom at Plum Gut.
body_markdown:
Tuesday night, max ebb, Plum Gut. I dropped a 12-inch eel off a three-way rig into the seam where the current stacks against the eastern edge of the rip, let it swing down and back like it's supposed to, and felt the rod load up like someone hooked a mooring ball. Forty seconds of pure deadlift and a 38-inch bass came up thrashing right at the transom. That's the fish that tells you everything about how this zone is fishing right now — deep, hard, and on gear built to survive current that doesn't care about your drag setting.

The pattern at the Gut and out at The Race hasn't changed much in two weeks, it's just gotten more precise. Bass are holding low, tight to the rock piles and current breaks, feeding almost exclusively when the water's ripping hardest — peak ebb and peak flood, the windows where the eddies behind Plum Island and the western edge of the Gut stack bait against structure. Shad-body swimbaits in the 6- to 9-inch range, white or bunker pattern, fished on jig heads heavy enough to hold bottom in five knots of current, have been money during those windows. When the current's screaming, I go to the three-way with a bucktail dropper and a big eel trailing behind — that combo has out-produced everything else I've thrown this month, and it's the same read that's been paying off for the shore guys working the rocks at 3 a.m.

New London's reading 67.6 degrees, which is a full four degrees cooler than what Kings Point's showing out west. That gradient matters more than people give it credit for. Western Sound bass have gone nocturnal — the water's warm enough that they're avoiding daylight stress and feeding almost exclusively after dark. Out here, with the water still in the mid-60s, we're not locked into that pattern yet. I've had fish hit at last light and again right at first light, not just in the dead of night. If you're planning a trip, that gives you two windows instead of one — work it.

The surprise this week was a 28-inch black sea bass that came off the same rip structure at Plum Gut, on a bucktail meant for bass. That's not a fluke — sea bass have moved onto that hard bottom in real numbers, stacking on the same rock piles and current breaks that hold the stripers. If you're fishing bucktails or diamond jigs down deep in the Gut right now, don't be shocked when something with a spiny dorsal fin nearly pulls your arm off. Keep a few Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged light for exactly that scenario.

Fluke fishing has been the most dependable thing out here, full stop. The Race, the flats off Orient Point, the drift lanes along Fishers Island — keeper fluke are showing consistently in 20 to 40 feet on the last two hours of the outgoing, with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails doing the damage on the drift. It's not a blitz, it's a grind — cover water, stay on bottom, work the seams where the current speeds up over the humps. But it's producing fish in the box every trip, which is more than I can say for some of the flashier bites right now.

Weakfish are worth a mention because they're some life on the calm, warm evenings — small numbers, but legal fish coming out of the same rip zones at dusk on bucktails and soft plastics fished slow near bottom. We flagged that rebuild coming on quiet evenings, and it's tracking. Not a target species yet, more of a bonus if you're already working the structure for bass.

Bluefish are the wildcard. The blitz action everyone's talking about — bunker schools getting hammered daily — is still concentrated west, from the Jersey beaches up through the western Sound. It hasn't pushed into Orient or Fishers Island Sound yet, but bunker schools have a way of migrating east through July, and if that bait shows up here, the blues will be right behind it. Keep an eye on the surface around Orient Point and the eastern flats — first sign of nervous water or diving birds, that's your cue.

Current's easing as we run toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which means softer tide stages through the weekend. That's going to change the presentation game — less need to muscle a heavy jig through five knots, more room to work a slower swimbait retrieve and actually work an eddy instead of just surviving it. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the Gut on the last half of Thursday's ebb, right as the moon phase starts softening the push. Have eels rigged heavy for the hard stages and a lighter swimbait rod ready for when it lays down. Bring a jig for the sea bass too — that bite's real, and it's a lot of fun on light tackle when the bass go quiet between current stages.
